food.text: The staples of the ancient Egyptian diet were bread and beer, supplemented with vegetables, legumes, fruits, meat and seasonings prepared in many ways. The cuisine retained many consistent traits over a span of more than three thousand years.

Mice and hedgehogs were also eaten in ancient Egypt. A common way to cook a hedgehog was to encase it in clay and bake it. When the clay was cracked open and removed, it took the prickly spikes with it.
Ancient Egyptians ate the tubers, stems and seeds of sedges, including papyrus, lotus and chufa. They were eaten raw, boiled or roasted, or ground into flour.

Bread and beer were usually prepared in the same places, because the yeast used for bread was also used for brewing. They were made either in special bakeries or, more often, at home, and any surplus would be sold.

Spices and herbs were added for flavor, but the spices were expensive imports and so were confined to the tables of the wealthy. Meats were mostly preserved by salting, and dates and raisins could be dried for long-term storage.

After bread and beer, vegetables and legumes were the main source of calories and nutrients for common and wealthy Egyptians alike. The most common vegetables were scallions or onions and garlic, and legumes included peas, beans, lentils, chickpeas, lobia and lupins.

Poultry, both wild and domestic, and fish were available to all but the most destitute. Other sources of protein would rather have been legumes, eggs, cheese and the amino acids available in the tandem staples of bread and beer.
Cheesemaking in Egypt dates back to the First Dynasty of Egypt. Domiati is the most popular type of cheese consumed there today, so a very old craft still shapes what Egyptians eat.

Bread is central to Nubian meals, and its origins trace back thousands of years. Archaeological findings at sites like Kerma illustrate this long history, and Nubian cooking is rooted in the agricultural practices of the Nile Valley.

Microscopy of beer residue points to a brewing method in which bread was not an ingredient. One batch of grain was sprouted and another cooked in water, the two were mixed, sieved, and then fermented with yeast. Most beers were made of barley and only a few of emmer wheat.
Mutton and pork were more common in ancient Egypt than one might expect. This was despite Herodotus' affirmations that swine were held by the Egyptians to be unclean and avoided.
A dessert was made from ground tiger nuts, the tuber of the chufa plant, mixed with honey. It shows that sweet dishes were part of the ancient Egyptian table.

art.text: The Old Kingdom is known as the Age of the Pyramids. King Sneferu perfected the art of pyramid-building, and his son Khufu commissioned the Great Pyramid of Giza, with which the fully developed pyramid style was reached.

Egyptians had mastered advanced shipbuilding as early as 3000 BC. Fourteen ships found at Abydos are the oldest planked ships known, made of wooden planks sewn together with woven straps, with reeds or grass stuffed between the planks to seal the seams.

Ancient Egyptians became very skilled at making jewelry from turquoise, gold, silver and small beads. Both men and women wore brightly colored earrings, bracelets, rings, necklaces and collars, and those who could not afford gold or stones made theirs from colored pottery beads.

The Fifth Dynasty began with Userkaf in 2494 BC and was marked by the growing importance of the cult of sun god Ra. Fewer efforts went into pyramid complexes than in the Fourth Dynasty, and more into sun temples at Abusir.

C-Group pottery from Lower Nubia is characterized by all-over incised geometric lines with white infill and impressed imitations of basketry. The C-group culture was typical of Lower Nubia from 2400 to 1650 BC.
The Bronze Age in Nubia started as early as 2300 BC. A furnace for bronze casting found in Kerma has been dated to 2300–1900 BC.

Rare etched carnelian beads found in Egypt are thought to have been imported from the Indus Valley Civilization through the Mesopotamian states of Sumer, Akkad and Assyria. Typically dated to the Late Middle Kingdom, around 1800 BCE, they were found in tombs. They were luxury items, often the centerpiece of jewelry.

Tradition credits Khafre, who commissioned the second pyramid at Giza, with the Great Sphinx. Egyptologist Vassil Dobrev has proposed instead that Djedefre commissioned it as a monument to his father Khufu.

Twelfth Dynasty pharaohs built a cluster of four mud-brick fortresses at the narrow Semna gorge: Semna, Kumma, Semna South and Uronarti. Lake Nasser now covers them. The temples of Dedwen and Sesostris III were moved to the National Museum of Sudan in Khartoum before the flooding.

The Hyksos ruler Khyan had wide-ranging contacts. A sphinx bearing his name was bought on the art market at Baghdad, and it might demonstrate diplomatic contacts with the Mesopotamian states of Assyria and Babylonia. It may even point to the first Kassite ruler, Gandash.

The C-Group people of Lower Nubia, who flourished from 2500 to 1500 BC, made distinctive pottery. It was decorated with all-over incised geometric lines filled with white, and with impressions that imitated basketry.

The 14 Abydos ships lie near a mortuary belonging to Pharaoh Khasekhemwy, so all were first thought to be his. One ship dates to 3000 BC and is 75 feet (23 m) long. It may have belonged to an earlier pharaoh, perhaps Hor-Aha.

Excavations at Semna found pottery sherds of the C-Group type, which suggest a peaceful coexistence between C-Group individuals and Egyptians. Seal impressions on numerous pieces of pottery included some bearing the name of the fort, which until then was only partially known. Translated by Dr. Žabkar, the name reads "Subduer of the Setiu-Nubians" or "Subduer of the Seti-land", which signifies Egypt's role in Nubia as ruler.

war.text: Before the New Kingdom, Egyptian armies were made up of conscripted peasants and artisans who massed under the pharaoh's banner. Soldiers carried a spear with a copper spearhead and a large wooden shield covered with leather hides. No armor was used during the 3rd and early 2nd Millennium BC.

Around 1600 BC the Egyptians fought and finally defeated the Hyksos, who had made themselves lords of Lower Egypt. The Hyksos brought the horse and chariot, and the Egyptians had no answer to them until they introduced their own war chariot at the beginning of the 18th Dynasty. They then improved the design to suit their own needs.

Around 2055 BC, Theban forces under Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II finally defeated the Herakleopolitan rulers, reuniting the Two Lands. The victory ended a period that began when the central government collapsed. Food shortages and political disputes escalated into famines and small-scale civil wars, and rival local rulers competed for territory and power. Severe droughts between 2200 and 2150 BC are believed to have helped cause this 140-year period of famine and strife, and the victory opened the Middle Kingdom, an era of economic and cultural renaissance.

The city-state of Kerma became the dominant political force in Nubia between 2450 and 1450 BC. It controlled the Nile Valley between the first and fourth cataracts, an area as large as Egypt. The Egyptians identified Kerma as "Kush", and the two civilizations engaged in intermittent warfare over the following centuries.

Around 1208 BC the pharaoh Merneptah won a decisive victory at the Battle of Perire over a coalition of Libyan tribes and Sea Peoples. The Great Karnak Inscription reports that he killed 6,000 Libyans, 2,201 Ekwesh, 722 Teresh and 200 Shekelesh, and captured 9,000 enemies, though Ian Shaw argued these numbers cannot be taken at face value because Egyptian inscriptions were prone to bombastic, exaggerated claims. Afterwards Merneptah ordered many of the captured enemies impaled south of Memphis, a brutal punishment rarely used in Egyptian history, apparently meant as a strong message to other potential Libyan invaders.

New Kingdom soldiers gained better gear after Egypt adopted bronze. Shields were now made from solid wood with a bronze buckle, and spears were tipped with a bronze point. The khopesh, a type of weapon, was adopted from Asiatic soldiers.

Egyptian King Thutmose I occupied Kush and destroyed its capital, Kerma, which led to Egypt annexing Nubia around 1504 BC. Around 1500 BC Nubia was absorbed into the New Kingdom, but rebellions continued for 220 years, until about 1300 BC. Nubia was governed as an Egyptian colony by a Viceroy of Kush.

A famine in Libya led tribes including the Tjehenu and Meshwesh to unite under a chief named Meryey. They hired or allied with Sea Peoples such as the Shekelesh, Teresh, Ekwesh, Lukka and Sherden. The Libyans possibly paid for these mercenaries with wealth gained from controlling trade from Central Africa to the Mediterranean Sea.

By 1900 BC, King Sesostris I began building a series of towns below the Second Cataract with heavy fortresses. These had enclosures and drawbridges. Later, Sesostris III raised massive river forts such as Buhen and Semna to control trade routes in Lower Nubia.

Egyptian fighting men left their own accounts. Ahmose, son of Ebana, served under Ahmose, Amenhotep I and Thutmose I, and wrote on his tomb-chapel walls of a campaign upstream. In it, "after his Majesty had slain the Bedoin of Asia, he sailed upstream to Upper Nubia to destroy the Nubian bowmen."

From the early Nineteenth Dynasty, fortresses were built west of modern-day Alexandria to shield the Nile Delta from Libyan incursions. At least one of them, Zawyet Umm El Rakham, was quickly abandoned. Ian Shaw argued this suggests Libyan tribes were pushing eastward, which ended in the invasion in Merneptah's reign.

Ramesses II campaigned against the wandering Shasu, pursuing them as far as Moab. There he established a fortress, after a near defeat at the Battle of Kadesh. Egyptian evidence shows the Shasu had been more problematic than the earlier ʿApiru since the reign of Horemheb.

Egyptian plunder lists after the Battle of Perire describe the spoils in great detail, even down to arrowheads. Yet they mention only the family of King Meryey, and no other women or children. Historian Konstantinos Kopanias therefore argued that the invaders were mainly soldiers, not large groups of dependants.

literature.text: Ancient Egyptian literature is considered, along with Sumerian literature, to be the world's earliest literature. By the Old Kingdom, from the 26th century BC to the 22nd century BC, it already included funerary texts, letters, hymns and poems, and autobiographical texts recounting officials' careers.

Narrative literature did not appear in Egypt until the early Middle Kingdom. Richard B. Parkinson calls this a "media revolution", driven by a rising intellectual class of scribes, new ideas about individuality, unprecedented literacy and wider access to written materials.

Some of the earliest known wisdom literature dates to the middle of the 3rd millennium BC and comes from ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt. Both regions kept producing wisdom literature for the next two and a half millennia.

Bronze Age cultures were the first to develop writing. Egypt, which used hieroglyphs, and Mesopotamia, which used cuneiform script, developed the earliest practical writing systems according to archaeological evidence.
Egyptian scribes worked out of an institution called the Per Ankh, or House of Life. It included offices, libraries called Houses of Books, laboratories and observatories.

Parkinson and Morenz argue that Old Kingdom texts mainly served to maintain divine cults, preserve souls in the afterlife and keep practical accounts. Only in the Middle Kingdom, from the early Twelfth Dynasty, were texts written for entertainment and intellectual curiosity.

Famous pieces such as the Pyramid and Coffin Texts were written in Classical Egyptian, which remained the language of writing until about 1300 BC. Late Egyptian, spoken from the New Kingdom onward, appears in Ramesside love poetry and tales.

The Egyptian genre called Sebayt, meaning 'instructions', passed on teachings and guidance from famous nobles. The Ipuwer papyrus, a poem of lamentations describing natural disasters and social upheaval, is a famous example.

Parkinson and Morenz speculate that Middle Kingdom written works were transcriptions of Old Kingdom oral literature. Some oral poetry is known to have survived in writing, since litter-bearers' songs were preserved as verses in Old Kingdom tomb inscriptions.
Egyptian writing developed the tomb autobiography, in which officials recorded their own careers. The tomb autobiographies of Harkhuf and Weni are well-known examples.

Model letters taken from dispatches sent to the Semna fortress of Nubia show the standardized epistolary formula of the late Middle Kingdom. They date to the reign of Amenemhat III, who ruled from 1860 to 1814 BC.

The first known complete sentence in Egyptian hieroglyphs is probably a seal impression from Peribsen's tomb, dating to about 2660 to 2650 BC. It reads: "Sealing of everything of Ombos: He of Ombos has joined the Two Lands for his son, the Dual King Peribsen."

The warrior Ahmose, son of Ebana, recorded his campaigns in autobiographical inscriptions on his tomb-chapel walls. He wrote that after slaying the Bedoin of Asia, the king sailed to Upper Nubia "to destroy the Nubian bowmen."

science.text: Copper metallurgy is attested at Kerma, in what is now Sudan, from about 2200 to 2000 BC. This falls within the Early Kerma period, when Kerma was a small fortified village that would later grow into a fortified settlement and then a fully urban center.

Around 3000 BC, agriculture developed and a cultural tradition began around Kerma. Kerma later grew into a large urban centre built around a big adobe temple, the Western Deffufa, which was built after 1750 BC.

The silt that fertilised Egypt's fields each year was brought down the Nile from the Ethiopian Highlands. Egyptian farmers developed basin irrigation to make use of the flood. Planting took place in October once the waters receded, and crops ripened between March and May. But the flood was not always kind: high floodwaters were destructive and could destroy irrigation canals, while a lack of flooding left Egyptians suffering from famine.

The 365 day period of the Egyptian calendar was already in use by the time the Dynastic Period began in the 3rd millennium BCE. Observing the stars was important for working out when the Nile's annual flood would arrive.

Ancient Egypt achieved a high standard of sophistication in technology, medicine and mathematics. The Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri, from about 1600 BC, are the evidence for what is first credited to Egypt as traditional empiricism.

Egyptian scribes could multiply two numbers using only doubling, halving and addition, with no multiplication table. The method breaks one number into powers of two and sums the matching doublings of the other. Essentially the same algorithm is still used in binary multiplier circuits in modern computer processors.
The Egyptians developed the Nilometer to measure the Nile's water level and the clarity of each year's flood. This helped forecast how the flood would affect the fields.

The rising of Sirius, called Sopdet in Egyptian and Sothis in Greek, at the beginning of the inundation was an especially important point to fix in the yearly calendar. Heliacal risings, the first appearances of stars at dawn, were of special interest for predicting the flood.

Chariots are believed to have been introduced to Egypt by the Hyksos invasion during the Second Intermediate Period, about 1650 to 1550 BC. During the New Kingdom, chariotry became central to Egypt's military.

Kerma began as a small, newly founded fortified village in the Early Kerma period. By 2000 to 1750 BC it was a fortified settlement of 3 hectares. In the Classic Kerma period (1750 to 1500 BC) it had grown into a fully urban settlement of about 25 hectares.

The pharaoh Amenemhet III of the Twelfth Dynasty, about 1800 BC, is evidenced as using the natural lake of the Fayûm as a reservoir. It stored surplus flood water for use during the dry seasons, since the lake swelled each year with the Nile's flooding.

The Book of Nut was one of the most important Egyptian astronomical texts, going back to the Middle Kingdom or earlier. Temple books also recorded the movements and phases of the Sun, Moon and stars, and astronomy helped fix festival dates and the hours of the night.

The ancient Egyptians laid out tables of many powers of two rather than recalculating them each time. To decompose a number, they found the largest power of two that fit, subtracted it and repeated until nothing remained. They did not use the number zero in mathematics.

The second Egyptian multiplication and division technique is known from the hieratic Moscow and Rhind Mathematical Papyri, written in the seventeenth century B.C. by the scribe Ahmes. Although base 2 did not exist as a concept in ancient Egypt, the algorithm matches long multiplication in binary.

Egyptians made wheel thrown pottery as early as the 4th Dynasty, about 2613 to 2494 BC. Flinders Petrie claimed lathes were used that early too, based on tool marks on stone bowls, though lathes are firmly known only from at least 1300 BC.

politics.text: Around 3150 BC, Upper and Lower Egypt were united by Menes, whom most Egyptologists believe to be the same person as Narmer. Afterward the country became known as the Two Lands, and a strong institution of kingship legitimized state control over its land, labor and resources.

Around 2055 BC, Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II and his Theban forces defeated the rulers of Herakleopolis, reuniting the Two Lands. This began the Middle Kingdom. His rivals had controlled Lower Egypt in the north, while his own Intef family had taken Upper Egypt in the south.

The Kerma culture of Nubia lasted from around 2500 BC until it was conquered by the New Kingdom of Egypt under Pharaoh Thutmose I around 1500 BC. Egyptian heirs then ruled much of Nubia for the next four centuries.

Warfare between Upper and Lower Egypt occurred often, and Narmer, reigning in Upper Egypt, defeated his enemies on the Delta and merged both kingdoms under his single rule. Palettes show Narmer wearing the double crown, made from the lotus flower for Upper Egypt and the papyrus reed for Lower Egypt. It was a sign of unified rule that all succeeding rulers followed.

Thutmose III expanded Egypt's army and used it to consolidate the empire built by his predecessors. This led to a peak of Egyptian power and wealth under Amenhotep III. The word pharaoh, originally the name of the king's palace, became a form of address for the king during this era.

Ramesses II, who reigned as the third ruler of the Nineteenth Dynasty, fathered around 100 children. He gave many heirs prominent positions as generals, governors and scribes, decentralising power among members of the royal family. He also oversaw the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty and moved the capital to Pi-Ramesses.

After Twosret, the last pharaoh of the 19th Dynasty, died, Egypt entered a period of civil war, attested by the Elephantine stela built by Setnakhte. Setnakhte ended the war by taking the throne and founding the 20th Dynasty. It is uncertain whether Twosret died peacefully or was overthrown by him.
The pharaohs of the Early Dynastic Period established a national administration and appointed royal governors. Before unification, the land had been settled with autonomous villages.

The Middle Kingdom of Egypt conquered Lower Nubia between 2000 and 1700 BC. By 1900 BC, Sesostris I was building a series of towns below the Second Cataract with heavy fortresses that had enclosures and drawbridges. Sesostris III relentlessly expanded his kingdom into Nubia from 1866 to 1863 BC and raised massive river forts such as Buhen and Semna to gain more control over the trade routes in Lower Nubia. The Egyptian garrisons seemed to coexist peacefully with the local Nubians, though they did not interact much with them.

After Merneptah's death, Seti II and Amenmesse both claimed the throne. Amenmesse overthrew Seti in the south, and some workers in Deir el-Medina were killed in the transfer of power, according to surviving documents. Seti II regained control of all Egypt by about 1198 BC and later portrayed Amenmesse as "the enemy" in his propaganda and murals. No record of Amenmesse survives beyond Seti's fifth year, which suggests his probable death.

Ramesses III's reign saw a harem conspiracy in which Queen Tiye, one of his lesser wives, was implicated in an assassination attempt. She wanted to put her son Pentawer on the throne. The king died from the attempt, but his legitimate heir Ramesses IV succeeded him and had approximately 30 conspirators put to death.

The Hyksos ruler Khyan had wide-ranging contacts, with objects bearing his name found at Knossos and Hattusha. A sphinx with his name was bought on the art market at Baghdad, and it might show diplomatic contacts with Assyria and Babylonia.

philosophy.text: Ancient Egyptian deities represented natural forces and phenomena. The Egyptians supported and appeased them through offerings and rituals so that these forces would keep functioning according to maat, or divine order. After the state was founded around 3100 BC, the pharaoh controlled the authority to perform these tasks.

In the reign of Akhenaten (c. 1353–1336 BC), a single solar deity, the Aten, became the sole focus of the state religion. Akhenaten stopped funding the temples of other gods and erased their names and images on monuments, targeting Amun in particular. The Aten had no mythology and was described in more abstract terms than traditional gods.

Atenism may not have been full monotheism. Evidence suggests ordinary people kept worshipping other gods in private, and Atenism apparently tolerated some deities such as Maat, Shu, and Tefnut. Egyptologists Dominic Montserrat and John Baines suggested Akhenaten may have been monolatrous, worshipping one deity while acknowledging others.

Egyptologist Jan Assmann described the Amarna theology of Akhenaten as a "monotheistic revolution". It held that the solar creation deity Aten was the only god, though it also drew on earlier developments such as the "New Solar Theology" based around Amun-Ra.

Heliopolis was the principal cult center of the solar deity Atum, who came to be identified with Ra. Its priests maintained that Atum or Ra was the first being, rising self-created from the primeval waters. A decline in Ra's cult during the Fifth Dynasty led to the Ennead, a grouping of nine major deities that placed the others in subordinate status to Ra–Atum.

After the Amarna period, Ramesside theology kept a focus on a single creative solar deity, but without outright rejecting other gods. Those gods came to be seen as manifestations of the main solar deity. This period also saw the development of the concept of the ba (soul) and its relation to god.

"The Dispute Between a Man and His Ba" is described as a masterpiece of the 19th century BC. In it a man laments "the misery of life", while his ba, his personality or soul, replies that life is good. The ba tells him to "ponder life", since it is a burial that is miserable.
tags: Dispute Between a Man and His Ba

philosophy.text: "The Teaching of Ani" was written in the 13th century BC by a humble middle-class scribe and gives advice to the ordinary man. Another text, "The Satire of the Trades" by Khety, tries to convince his son Pepy to "love books more than your mother", since nothing "on earth" compares to being a scribe.

A gold solar boat model from the tomb of Queen Ahhotep, from about 1550 BC, was mounted on four-spoked chariot wheels. Similarities have been noted with the Trundholm Sun Chariot from Denmark, dated c. 1500–1400 BC, which was also mounted on four-spoked wheels.

According to Goldwasser (2006), the Hyksos king Apophis (c. 1550 BC) may have been the first to introduce into the history of ideas the option of a "single god and no other". She calls this the first step on the long winding road of monotheism.

culture.text: The Pan-Grave culture takes its name from the pan-shaped graves in which its people were buried. The body was typically placed in a crouched position on its right side, along with handmade bowls, animal skulls and Egyptian-style weapons. The culture dates from about 1850 to 1600 BCE.

Egyptian art distinguished the people of Kush by their dress, appearance and even their method of transportation. Yet Kush had also developed cultural affinities with Egypt, such as the veneration of Amun, and the royal families of the two kingdoms occasionally intermarried.

In February 2020, Egyptian archaeologists uncovered 83 tombs dating back to 3,000 BC, in the Naqada III period. The burials held small ceramic pots, sea shells, makeup tools, eyeliner pots and jewels.

Major pharaonic ceremonies were held at Jebel Barkal near Napata, after Nubia was absorbed into the New Kingdom of Egypt around 1500 BC. Nubia became a key province of Egypt economically, politically and spiritually. It was governed by an Egyptian Viceroy of Kush.

Two golden statuettes found at Tell el-Farkha show standing naked men, one 60 cm tall and the other 30 cm, with bald heads, large protruding ears and unnaturally large phalluses. Both wear very large phallus sheaths, and one sheath is decorated with a carved band. They most probably depict a Predynastic ruler and his son during the heb-sed festival, and probably adorned a shrine in the Western Kom area. They are thought to date to Naqada IIIB, c. 3200 to 3000 BC, and to be the oldest known depictions of ancient Egyptian rulers.

At Aniba, ancient Miam, the temple of Horus of Miam stood within the town, and a Nubian village of the C-Group culture lay to the north. Huge cemeteries surrounded the town, with some tombs built in purely Egyptian style. It is not known whether their occupants were Nubians who adopted Egyptian culture or native Egyptians.

Fourteen ships found at Abydos were built of wooden planks sewn together with woven straps, and reeds or grass stuffed between the planks sealed the seams. One ship dates to 3000 BC and was 75 feet (23 m) long. It may have belonged to an early pharaoh, perhaps Hor-Aha.

The only text definitively linked to the Pan-Grave culture was found at the large cemetery at Mostagedda. It consists of six Egyptian hieroglyphs painted on an ox skull, in a grave holding only goat and cow remains. Together with Egyptian-style artwork, burial customs and pottery, it suggests a high level of syncretism.

Rare etched carnelian beads found in Egypt are thought to have come from the Indus Valley Civilization via Mesopotamian states. Found in tombs and dating to about 1800 BCE, they were luxury items, often the centerpiece of jewelry.
